title: Radial Migration: Climbing the Glial Ladder

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: List the main zones a newborn excitatory cortical neuron passes through from its ventricular birthplace to its settling region, omitting the subplate.
cards.back: Ventricular zone → subventricular zone → intermediate zone → cortical plate.
cards.quote: The main zones, from the inside out (the subplate, between the intermediate zone and the cortical plate, is left out)

cards.front: The cell body of a migrating neuron, which contains its nucleus, is called the {{c1::soma}}.
cards.quote: a cell body, or soma, that holds the nucleus.

cards.front: What is the centrosome, and where does it usually sit in a migrating cortical neuron?
cards.back: The main microtubule-organizing centre; near the nucleus or a little ahead of it in the leading process.
cards.quote: The centrosome, the cell's main organizing centre for microtubules, sits near the nucleus or a little ahead of it in the leading process.

cards.front: Why must neuronal migration be measured at the nucleus relative to surrounding tissue?
cards.back: A leading process can grow while the soma stays put. Nuclear displacement relative to tissue shows that the cell body has advanced.
cards.quote: Migration is measured at the nucleus, relative to the tissue, not at the tip.

cards.front: During imaging, a neuronal nucleus and nearby tissue landmarks shift together, keeping their separation unchanged. What happens to the measured migration relative to tissue, and why?
cards.back: It remains zero: the nucleus has not changed position relative to the tissue. Movement across the image alone does not establish migration.
cards.quote: You would need to see the soma, and so its nucleus, move relative to the surrounding tissue.

cards.front: How do somal translocation and locomotion differ in process attachment and soma movement in developing mouse cortex?
cards.back: Translocation: in many cells, the soma moves fairly smoothly within a shortening process attached near the pia. Locomotion: a shorter, freely ending process leads a soma that advances in jumps.
cards.quote: Picture translocation as a person on a rope that is already tied to the ceiling, simply reeling in.

cards.front: A developing mouse cortex thickens from an early to a later stage. Which radial migration mode becomes more prominent, and why?
cards.back: Locomotion becomes more prominent: the stage-dependent pattern shifts from early translocation within a long surface-attached process to later movement in jumps behind a shorter, free process.
cards.quote: Locomotion, the harder case, is where the front and the nucleus come apart, and most of this lesson is about it.

cards.front: What two roles do radial glia serve in cortical development?
cards.back: They are the main cortical progenitors and provide fibres that migrating neurons can climb.
cards.quote: The fibres the neurons climb belong to radial glia. As the lesson on radial glia explains, these same cells are the main progenitors of the cortex.
cards.section: The glial ladder: from an inference to a movie

cards.front: Why does a fixed image of a neuron touching a glial fibre support contact more strongly than movement along the fibre?
cards.back: It captures position and contact at one moment. It cannot reveal which cell moved or the sequence of movement.
cards.quote: It showed contact, and it suggested a climb, but it could not show which cell moved, or how.
cards.section: The glial ladder: from an inference to a movie

cards.front: Live imaging shows neurons moving along glial fibres in culture. Design a test of whether those fibres are required, and state what remains unproven about the living brain.
cards.back: Compare nuclear movement relative to the coverslip with intact guides versus removed or disabled guides. Reduced movement would support a requirement in that preparation; a culture result alone would still leave necessity in the living brain unproven. This uses the distinction between observing a possible route and testing necessity.
cards.quote: It did not show that glia are required in the living brain, or what tells a neuron to get off.
cards.section: The glial ladder: from an inference to a movie

cards.front: What did movies of recombined postnatal mouse cerebellar granule neurons and astroglia establish about the relation between tip growth and soma movement?
cards.back: Neurons could migrate along glial processes in stop-and-go steps; leading-tip extension and retraction occurred out of step with soma movement.
cards.quote: a leading tip that extended and retracted out of step with the soma.
cards.section: The glial ladder: from an inference to a movie

cards.front: Forward movement of the nucleus during neuronal migration is called {{c1::nucleokinesis}}.
cards.quote: Nucleokinesis, the forward movement of the nucleus, works as a "two stroke" cycle.

cards.front: What is the order of leading process, centrosome and nucleus movement in the usual two-stroke locomotion cycle?
cards.back: The leading process extends and forms a swelling; the centrosome enters it; then the nucleus advances into it and the trailing cell follows.
cards.quote: So the proposed order is front, then centrosome, then nucleus.

cards.front: How does the microtubule cage link the nucleus to the centrosome in the usual model of neuronal locomotion?
cards.back: Microtubules wrap around the nucleus and run forward toward the centrosome, providing tracks along which nuclear dynein can bring the nucleus forward.
cards.quote: bundles of microtubules wrapped around the nucleus like a cage, with the microtubules running forward toward the centrosome.

cards.front: In the usual two-stroke model, a cortical neuron forms a swelling, but its centrosome fails to advance into it. What happens to the expected nuclear step, and why?
cards.back: The usual nuclear step should be impaired: the second stroke normally carries the nucleus toward a centrosome that has already advanced. This prediction uses the front–centrosome–nucleus sequence.
cards.quote: Dynein on the surface of the nucleus walks along the cage and carries the nucleus toward the centrosome, which now sits ahead.
cards.section: The engine: what brings the nucleus up

cards.front: Cytoplasmic dynein walks toward microtubule {{c1::minus ends}}.
cards.quote: The motor is cytoplasmic dynein, which walks toward minus ends, that is, toward the centrosome.
cards.section: The engine: what brings the nucleus up

cards.front: Why can the same dynein motor either move cargo or move a microtubule?
cards.back: Movable cargo attached to dynein travels toward minus ends. If dynein is anchored, it instead drags the microtubule toward its attachment site.
cards.quote: If dynein is held in place, it cannot walk anywhere, so it drags the microtubule instead,
cards.section: The engine: what brings the nucleus up

cards.front: In the usual neuronal locomotion model, how does dynein perform different jobs in the two strokes?
cards.back: At the swelling, dynein pulls microtubules and the centrosome forward. At the nucleus, dynein carries the nucleus along the cage toward the advanced centrosome.
cards.quote: The microtubule network, and with it the centrosome, is drawn forward into the swelling.
cards.section: The engine: what brings the nucleus up

cards.front: What is LIS1’s role in the dynein machinery of a migrating cortical neuron?
cards.back: It binds and regulates dynein in both strokes; it is not itself the motor.
cards.quote: LIS1 binds dynein and regulates it in both places; it is not the motor itself.
cards.section: The engine: what brings the nucleus up

cards.front: LIS1 is knocked down in migrating neurons in embryonic rat cortical slices. What happens to the centrosome and nucleus while the tip keeps extending, and why?
cards.back: Both centrosome and nucleus stall: LIS1 loss impairs dynein’s proposed jobs in both strokes. Continued tip extension therefore does not show continued migration.
cards.quote: Knocking down LIS1 or dynein impairs both of dynein's proposed jobs, and both the centrosome and the nucleus stall.
cards.section: The engine: what brings the nucleus up

cards.front: A myosin II inhibitor stops neuronal cell bodies while leading processes keep growing. What does this perturbation support about the requirements for those two movements?
cards.back: Soma advance requires myosin II activity under these conditions, whereas process extension can continue despite its inhibition. The movements have separable requirements.
cards.quote: When Schaar and McConnell added it, leading processes could keep growing while the cell bodies stopped.
cards.section: The engine: what brings the nucleus up

cards.front: For fixed nuclear steps, mean migration speed equals step per cycle multiplied by {{c1::cycles per hour}}.
cards.quote: If each cycle moves the nucleus a fixed step, mean speed = step per cycle × cycles per hour

cards.front: In a toy model, a neuronal nucleus steps 6 micrometres every 15 minutes. How long does it take to cross 48 micrometres of tissue, and what is its mean speed?
cards.back: Steps = 48/6 = 8; time = 8 × 15 = 120 minutes = 2 hours. Mean speed = 48/2 = 24 micrometres per hour.
cards.quote: A nucleus that advances 6 micrometres per cycle, with one cycle every 15 minutes, travels 6 × 4 = 24 micrometres an hour.

cards.front: A neuronal soma moves at about 56 micrometres per hour during bursts and about 33 micrometres per hour overall. Assuming it is stationary between bursts, what fraction of time is it moving?
cards.back: Mean speed = moving fraction × burst speed. Moving fraction = 33/56 ≈ 0.589, or about 59% (roughly 60%).
cards.quote: If a cell moved only at burst speed and stood still the rest of the time, it would be moving 33 ÷ 56, about 60 percent of the time.

cards.front: In a toy model, control and treated tips each advance 24 micrometres per hour for 2 hours. The control nucleus steps 6 micrometres every 15 minutes; the treated nucleus stays still. How does each tip-to-nucleus distance change, and what would tip-only scoring miss?
cards.back: Each tip advances 24 × 2 = 48 micrometres. Control nuclear advance = (120/15) × 6 = 48 micrometres, so its gap has no net change. Treated nuclear advance = 0, so its gap grows by 48 micrometres. Tip-only scoring would miss failed soma migration. The rule is to measure migration at the nucleus relative to tissue.
cards.quote: Tracked at the tip, the two cells look the same, and you would score the knockdown as a normal migrator.

cards.front: A cortex with reduced or absent folding is described as {{c1::lissencephaly}}.
cards.back: In the classic form, it is also abnormally thick and poorly layered because neurons failed to reach their places.
cards.quote: Lissencephaly means a cortex with reduced or absent folding;

cards.front: How can a DCX mutation interfere with the machinery of nuclear migration?
cards.back: DCX encodes doublecortin, which binds and stabilizes microtubules. Its disruption affects the tracks used by the nuclear movement machinery.
cards.quote: It encodes a protein that binds and stabilizes microtubules, the tracks the engine runs on.

cards.front: Why can a girl heterozygous for a DCX mutation develop subcortical band heterotopia?
cards.back: Random X inactivation creates a mosaic: neurons using normal DCX migrate, while some using mutant DCX stall, forming grey matter within white matter below the cortex.
cards.quote: Girls with one mutant copy are mosaics, because each cell switches off one of its two X chromosomes at random:

cards.front: A boy carries a DCX mutation on his X chromosome. Compared with a girl heterozygous for that mutation, what cortical phenotype is typical, and why?
cards.back: Lissencephaly is typical in boys. A heterozygous girl can instead form a grey-matter band because random X inactivation creates migrating and stalled neuronal populations.
cards.quote: Boys with a mutation typically have lissencephaly.

cards.front: How does Cdk5 sit upstream of nuclear migration machinery?
cards.back: Activated in neurons by p35 or p39, Cdk5 phosphorylates targets including NDEL1, a dynein regulator working with LIS1, and doublecortin.
cards.quote: Among its targets are NDEL1, a dynein regulator that works with LIS1, and doublecortin, so Cdk5 sits upstream of the same nuclear machinery.

cards.front: A mouse with a candidate nuclear-migration defect still has a smooth cortex. Which readouts would better assess a defect, and why?
cards.back: Measure neuronal migration speed and final positions, including cortical layering. The normal mouse cortex is already smooth, so loss of folds is not a useful readout.
cards.quote: In a mouse you look at how fast neurons move and where they end up, for example whether the cortical layers are disordered.

cards.front: How does the multipolar stage alter the route of newborn neurons filmed in embryonic rat cortical slices?
cards.back: After reaching the subventricular zone, cells linger multipolar with little net outward progress; many temporarily move ventricleward before becoming bipolar and migrating to the cortical plate.
cards.quote: Many then moved back toward the ventricle for a time before turning bipolar and migrating radially to the cortical plate.

cards.front: A multipolar neuron shows little net outward progress during an imaging interval. What happens to the claim that it is immobile, and why?
cards.back: That claim is unsupported: a multipolar neuron can move slowly, change direction and pause while making little net outward progress. Net displacement alone can hide movement.
cards.quote: It extends and retracts several processes and can move slowly, changing direction, between pauses.

cards.front: After LIS1 knockdown in embryonic rat cortex, fewer neurons reach the cortical plate. Can this endpoint alone identify failure of the second stroke in bipolar locomotion? Propose a better readout.
cards.back: No. LIS1 loss can affect progenitor nuclear movement, the multipolar-to-bipolar transition and soma advance. Film cells through these stages and, during bipolar locomotion, track centrosomes and nuclei separately. The rule is that a gene acting at several stages cannot be assigned to one failed step from final position alone.
cards.quote: LIS1 knockdown in embryonic rat cortex blocks the nuclear movement of progenitors, the multipolar-to-bipolar change and the movement of the soma,

cards.front: In embryonic rat cortical slices, a treatment preserves tip extension but stops nuclei. Design an imaging readout to distinguish impaired LIS1/dynein activity from a myosin II block.
cards.back: Track centrosomes and nuclei separately. Stalling of both supports the LIS1/dynein pattern; continued centrosome advance with nuclear stalling supports the myosin II pattern. The inference combines the two-stroke machinery with perturbation results and should be checked against controls in the same preparation.
cards.quote: LIS1 or dynein knockdown stalls both the centrosome and the nucleus, while a myosin II block stops only the nucleus,

cards.front: Knockdown of a gene stalls neuronal soma movement. Expression of a knockdown-resistant copy restores movement. What does this rescue add to the interpretation?
cards.back: It supports the link between loss of that gene’s function and the movement defect. Restoring the targeted function reverses the phenotype, strengthening the causal interpretation.
cards.quote: As a control, add blebbistatin to normal cells and check that it reproduces the second pattern, and rescue the first with a knockdown-resistant LIS1.

cards.front: A long myosin II block eventually stalls both centrosomes and nuclei in cortical neurons. Does that late pattern uniquely identify a primary dynein defect? Explain using the migration model and its limits.
cards.back: No. The systems interact, so prolonged inhibition of one may slow the other. The initial differential movement pattern is more informative than a late shared arrest, and comparisons require matched cell types and perturbation strength. This rests on the model’s separable strokes plus its stated interaction and context limits.
cards.quote: The two systems interact, and a long block in either may slow the other.

cards.front: Rat neuroblasts complete a nuclear step after microtubules are disrupted only after a swelling forms, yet cortical LIS1/dynein knockdown stalls migration. Why do these results not establish that microtubules are dispensable for migration?
cards.back: Completing one prepared step does not test building the swelling or sustaining repeated cycles. The preparations and intervention timing also differ. The rule is to distinguish a stage-specific result from a requirement across the full two-stroke cycle; the knockdown work still supports essential microtubule/dynein functions.
cards.quote: once a swelling had formed, the nucleus still advanced after nocodazole disrupted microtubules, and blebbistatin blocked that step;

cards.front: In a large primate cortex, you find radial glia with no ventricular contact. What happens to the inference that these cells cannot contribute migration fibres, and why?
cards.back: It fails: outer radial glia lack ventricular contact yet add fibres in the large primate cortex. Ventricular attachment is not required for this contribution.
cards.quote: In the large primate cortex, outer radial glia, which have no ventricular contact, add more fibres.

cards.front: How does nuclear movement in radial glial progenitors differ from the two-stroke advance of a migrating neuron?
cards.back: Progenitor nuclei move away from the ventricle in G1 and return in G2 before ventricular division; migrating neurons advance centrosome and nucleus in the same direction.
cards.quote: In interkinetic nuclear migration the nucleus of a radial glial cell moves away from the ventricle in G1 and back to it in G2,
